scenarios.title: The Record Chase
scenarios.text: You're close to an all-time kicking record, and the league has noticed: a counter on the broadcast graphics, a camera crew at practice, and a stranger at the gas station who knows the exact number.

choices.label: Never talk about the number
choices.result: The number stays out of every interview and every conversation in the building. The specialists guard it like a secret, and you sleep better than the reporters do.

choices.label: Enjoy the attention
choices.result: For once you enjoy it: the crew, the stranger at the gas station, the kids holding signs with the number on them. It's fun, and the record doesn't care either way.

choices.label: Share it with the old unit
choices.result: The old specialists you came up with get a call and an invitation to a game. They come, all of them, and sit together in the stands wearing jerseys from three different clubs.

choices.label: Remember the scouting report
choices.result: You dig out the old scouting report that called you 'accurate but limited' and pin it in your locker. It's the best motivational speech you've ever read.
choices.lock_text: having been scouted as an accuracy kicker

scenarios.title: The Former Teammate's Induction
scenarios.text: A former teammate is going into the Hall of Fame, and he's asked you to sit with his family at the ceremony. The speech he's written mentions you twice, once for a kick and once for something you'd forgotten.

choices.label: Go and sit with the family
choices.result: In the third row, in a borrowed suit, you sit with his family. When he mentions you, his mother squeezes your arm, and you realize you're crying too.

choices.label: Send a gift instead
choices.result: A practice game day, so you send a framed photo of the two of you as rookies instead. He puts it on the stage beside the podium, and the cameras find it.

choices.label: Ask what you did
choices.result: You call him before the ceremony and ask what the forgotten thing was. It was a ride home after a terrible game, years ago, and he says it changed everything for him.

choices.label: Laugh about the rides
choices.result: You laugh together about the rides home you used to give in college, and how you never stopped. He says it's why he asked you, and neither of you says much else.
choices.lock_text: having driven teammates home in college

scenarios.title: The Friend's Retirement
scenarios.text: A close friend in the league announces his retirement on a Tuesday morning, with a short post and a photo of his cleats. He texts you an hour later: 'Your turn to be the old guy now.'

choices.label: Drive to see him
choices.result: You drive four hours to see him on your day off and spend the afternoon on his porch. He's lighter than you've ever seen him, and it scares you a little.

choices.label: Text back a joke
choices.result: A joke back about his cleats and his new career in golf. He sends back a photo from a golf course an hour later, and the thread runs all week.

choices.label: Ask him how he knew
choices.result: You ask him how he knew it was time. His answer is long and honest, and you read it three times in the parking lot before you go in.

scenarios.title: The Agent's Final Pitch
scenarios.text: Your agent works the phones for one more opportunity, and calls you every evening with the list: two clubs interested, one maybe, and one that wants a workout before it says anything.

choices.label: Take the workout
choices.result: A workout, at your age, in front of three coaches with clipboards. It's humbling and hard, and you kick better than they expected, which is the point.

choices.label: Wait for a real offer
choices.result: No workouts, only real offers. Your agent sighs, then respects it, and the 'maybe' turns into a 'yes' a week later.

choices.label: Tell your agent to slow down
choices.result: You ask your agent to slow down and let you think about whether you want any of them. It's the first honest conversation you've had about the end.

choices.label: Make the calls yourself
choices.result: The calls are yours to make, the way they have been for years. Two of the clubs are surprised to hear your voice, and one of them makes an offer on the spot.
choices.lock_text: having fired an agent and handled your own deals

scenarios.title: The Team's Salary Decision
scenarios.text: The front office is deciding whether your experience is still worth your salary. Your agent has heard it from a friend of a friend, and the general manager hasn't returned a call in a week.

choices.label: Offer to take less
choices.result: You offer to take less money to stay, through your agent, before they ask. The club accepts with visible relief, and your standing in the building rises.

choices.label: Make them decide on the field
choices.result: The field makes the argument for you: every practice charted, every kick clean. The front office decides in your favor at the end of camp, at the same salary.

choices.label: Ask for a meeting
choices.result: You ask for a meeting with the general manager and get one the next day. It's frank and fair, and you leave knowing exactly what the numbers look like.

choices.label: Tell them you don't need the money
choices.result: You tell the general manager you don't need the money, because you saved it years ago, and you'll play for what's fair. It changes the whole conversation in your favor.

scenarios.title: The Younger Kicker's Challenge
scenarios.text: A rookie says it to your face in the locker room, loud enough for the whole row to hear: 'With respect, you can't compete anymore.' The room goes quiet, and every head turns to see what you'll do.

choices.label: Laugh and invite him outside
choices.result: You laugh and invite him outside for a kicking contest, ten kicks each, right then. The contest becomes the story of camp, and he's buying your lunch for a week.

choices.label: Say nothing and work
choices.result: Nothing, not a word. You just show up the next morning an hour early and every morning after, and the rookie stops saying it by the second week.

choices.label: Ask him why he thinks so
choices.result: You ask him, seriously, why he thinks so. His answer is half right, and you tell him so, and the conversation turns into the best mentoring of your career.

choices.label: Hold the line
choices.result: Calmly, in front of the room, you tell him that respect in this building is earned by work, not by age or noise. He nods, red-faced, and apologizes at lunch.
choices.lock_text: having held teammates accountable in college

scenarios.title: The Old Stadium
scenarios.text: A road game at the stadium where you kicked for the first time as a pro. The tunnel smells the same, the visitors' locker room still has the same broken hook, and the same old security guard waves you through.

choices.label: Walk the field alone
choices.result: You walk the field alone the night before, slowly, end zone to end zone. It's quiet and strange, and you remember the rookie who walked it shaking.

choices.label: Find the security guard
choices.result: The old security guard remembers you, and you talk for twenty minutes about the years in between. He shows you a photo of you as a rookie that he's kept in his wallet.

choices.label: Hang your jacket on the broken hook
choices.result: You hang your jacket on the same broken hook, on purpose, for luck. The young specialists ask why, and you tell them the whole story of your first day.

scenarios.title: The Jersey Recognition
scenarios.text: The first club that ever signed you wants to honor your career at halftime next month, whether or not you're still wearing their colors. They want a speech, a video and your family on the field.

choices.label: Give the speech
choices.result: A short speech, rewritten nine times, with names in it. The crowd stands, and the old equipment manager cries in the tunnel and denies it afterwards.

choices.label: Bring the family onto the field
choices.result: You bring {parent} and {sibling} onto the field and let them take the applause. {parent} waves to the crowd like a politician, and the clip runs for a week.

choices.label: Ask them to honor someone else
choices.result: You ask them to honor the trainer and the snapper from your rookie year alongside you. The club agrees, and the three of you walk out together.

choices.label: Invite the person you made peace with
choices.result: You invite the person you made peace with years ago, and they come. Seeing them in the stands that night means more than the video, and you tell them so.

scenarios.title: The Retirement Interview
scenarios.text: A broadcaster asks you for a retirement date, on air, during a live pregame segment. The camera is close, the red light is on, and there's no polite way out of the question.

choices.label: Give a straight answer
choices.result: The straight answer: when the leg says so, and not a day before. The broadcaster laughs, the clip is short, and nobody asks again for the rest of the month.

choices.label: Turn it into a joke
choices.result: You give a fake date, very specific, years in the future, and a fake reason. The internet decides it's the funniest thing you've ever said, and the broadcaster plays along.

choices.label: Turn the question around
choices.result: When is the broadcaster retiring, you ask right back, on air. The studio erupts, the segment runs long, and the two of you end up friends for the rest of your career.

choices.label: Answer like a host
choices.result: You answer like the host you used to be: a pause, a story and a punchline. The broadcaster asks, off air, whether you'd want their job someday.
choices.lock_text: having hosted your own radio show

scenarios.title: The Specialists Job
scenarios.text: A club calls with an offer: coach its specialists, starting next season, with a staff office, a parking space and a contract that runs longer than any you've signed as a player.

choices.label: Take it seriously
choices.result: You visit the facility, meet the staff and ask every question you can think of. You don't decide yet, but for the first time you can picture the life after.

choices.label: Say not yet
choices.result: Not yet, you tell them, with thanks. They say the offer stands, and you go back to practice lighter, knowing a door is open.

choices.label: Coach on the side
choices.result: You offer to help their young specialists on your days off, unpaid, to see if you like it. You love it, which surprises you, and the kids improve.

choices.label: Ask what they really want
choices.result: You ask what they really want from a coach, honestly, the way you once asked your own coaches. The answer is clear and specific, and it helps you decide.
choices.lock_text: having asked coaches for honesty in college

scenarios.title: The Broadcasting Contract
scenarios.text: A network offers you a full-time broadcasting job: color commentary, twelve weekends a year, starting whenever you stop playing. The contract is sitting in your email, and it has a deadline.

choices.label: Sign it for later
choices.result: You sign it for later, with a start date that says 'upon retirement'. It's a strange relief to know what comes next, and you kick looser all month.

choices.label: Ask for a trial
choices.result: A trial broadcast first, on a bye week, in a booth with a veteran announcer. You're nervous and good, and the network extends the deadline happily.

choices.label: Let the deadline pass
choices.result: The deadline passes, politely, with your thanks. You're a kicker, for now, and you want to finish being one before you start being anything else.

choices.label: Call your old producer
choices.result: You call your old radio producer, who reads the contract and finds two bad clauses. The network fixes both, and you sign a much better deal for later.
choices.lock_text: having hosted your own radio show

scenarios.title: The Family Reunion
scenarios.text: Your family wants to celebrate your career together: a reunion in a rented hall, cousins flying in, old photos on poster boards, and {parent} working on a speech in secret.

choices.label: Go all in
choices.result: You go all in: the hall, the photos, a slideshow you secretly help with. {parent}'s speech is long and funny and wrong about half the dates, and it's perfect.

choices.label: Make it small
choices.result: A smaller version, at home, with the people who matter most. It's quieter and warmer, and {sibling} tells the story of your first kick in the backyard.

choices.label: Wait until you've retired
choices.result: You ask them to wait until you've actually retired. They agree, a little disappointed, and {parent} keeps the speech in a drawer.

choices.label: Thank them for the early years
choices.result: You stand up and thank them for the years before the money, when the family went without so you could go to camps. Nobody in the hall has dry eyes.
choices.lock_text: having paid off the family's debt

scenarios.title: The Empty House
scenarios.text: The house is very quiet this week: the kids are away with {parent}, the dog is asleep on the stairs, and you notice for the first time how loud the kitchen clock is.

choices.label: Enjoy the quiet
choices.result: You enjoy the quiet: long sleeps, film on the couch, a book finished in two nights. Your body thanks you, and you miss the noise more than you expected.

choices.label: Call the kids every night
choices.result: A call every night, longer than the kids want, full of questions about their day. {parent} says they talk about you constantly when you're not on the phone.

choices.label: Fix up their rooms
choices.result: The week goes into fixing up the kids' rooms: new shelves, a fresh coat of paint, a surprise for each of them. They come home to it and shriek.
